newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - French growth jumps, govt target in reach.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - French growth jumps, govt target in reach.

text.p: A robust acceleration in the pace of French economic growth in the third quarter put the government's 1996 growth forecast within reach but economists said the economy remained fragile.
Gross domestic product (GDP) rose 0.9 percent after a revised decline of 0.2 percent in the second quarter, national statistics institute INSEE reported on Thursday.

It had initially reported a 0.4 percent fall in the second quarter and the new figures mean that, even if the economy does not expand in the last three months of the year, annual growth will be 1.2 percent, near the official 1.3 percent prediction.
French finance minister Jean Arthuis said, "The government's forecast of 1.3 percent growth therefore appears plausible."

Demand for cars ahead of the expiry of a government subsidy scheme at the end of September was the driving force behind the third quarter rise and a technical adjustment for the number of working days in the period flattered the headline figure, economists said.

"The dynamics of the scenario are still weak and we won't see year-on-year growth of more than 1.5 percent until the second quarter of 1997 at best," Joanne Perez, strategist at Merrill Lynch in Paris, said.
The figures released on Thursday showed the French economy expanded 1.4 percent in the third quarter from the same period a year earlier after a 0.7 percent rise in the second quarter.
"Nothing has really changed the overall picture," she said. "Take cars and the working day effect away and there's not much left."

INSEE said a 1.0 percent rise in consumption in the third quarter, spending on cars was up 13.6 percent, and the fact there were more working days than the second quarter accounted for 0.85 percentage points of the overall 0.9 percent increase.
Economists said they expected a weak final quarter but that the worst of the economy's weakness may be over.
"The overall picture is that as in Germany, the economy has touched bottom," Christopher Potts, chief economist Cheuvreux de Virieu, said.

"We will have a weak fourth quarter in terms of numbers. I think the number will be flat," he said. "It is not even impossible that we could have a negative GDP number in the fourth quarter, but it doesn't change the big picture."
Patrick Mange, economist at Deutsche Bank in Paris, said "We could come out best at 0.1 percent in the fourth quarter but we could equally drop 0.2 percent."

A harbinger of a gloomier fourth quarter came on Tuesday with figures showing consumer spending on manufactured goods fell a larger-than-expected 2.6 percent in October with a 25.8 percent slump in car sales fueling the drop.

Economist said the one surprise in Thursday's GDP release was a 1.0 percent rise in investment by private companies, the first increase seen since the third quarter last year, although most were sceptical about the sustainability of the turnaround.
"It is a very fragile first estimate," Potts said. "After the news we have had over the past year it is to be taken with some caution.That will be the last component of demand to turn."
Perez at Merrill Lynch said the fact recent business surveys showed the level of plant use by French companies remained low suggested there was little need for major investment.
"There's no widespread movement towards investment, I don't think there's any sector under pressure to invest," she said.

She also said that besides hitting production temporarily, the ongoing French truck drivers strike could sap business confidence and lead to a reluctance among firms to rebuild levels of inventories, all weighing on fourth quarter growth.
"If anything I might revise down from fourth quarter forecast." she said.
